Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Recognize the most common type of proximal metaphyseal tibia fracture.
Identify fractures at risk for complications, such as malunion and compartment syndrome.
Review factors that influence the management of pediatric tibial shaft fractures.
Proximal Tibia Metaphyseal Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
Proximal tibia fractures through the metaphysis usually occur in younger children, typically
those aged 3 to 6 years.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Vascular Anatomy
The distal portion of the popliteal artery lies in close proximity to the posterior aspect of the
proximal tibia and is tethered to the knee capsule by thick connective tissue.
The popliteal artery divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
The anterior tibial artery pierces the interosseous membrane and runs with the deep
peroneal nerve within the anterior compartment.
The posterior tibial artery runs adjacent to the tibial nerve within the deep posterior
compartment.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The most common mechanism of injury is a low-energy valgus force across an extended knee.
Torus (compression) and complete fractures may occur in this region but are far less common.
High-energy injuries may result from motor vehicle collisions and falls from a height.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
If a low-energy force is applied to the lateral aspect of an extended knee, the medial
aspect of the proximal tibia fails in tension, typically creating an incomplete greenstick
fracture. Classically, these injuries result from children going down a slide with the leg
extended, in the lap of an adult. The fibula usually is not injured; however, plastic
deformation may be observed.
Associated Injuries
Associated are uncommon in this age group.
Injury Classification
No specific classification system is used.
Mechanics of Fractures

Many sources combine multiple proximal metaphyseal tibia fractures (eg, greenstick, torus,
displaced) under the category of Cozen fractures.
However, Cozen1 originally described a nondisplaced proximal tibia fracture with complete
fracture through the medial cortex and a greenstick or buckle fracture of the lateral cortex
with valgus angulation.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Children usually present with refusal to bear weight and pain and tenderness in the region of
the fracture or deformity.
Minimal soft-tissue swelling or deformity usually is noted on physical examination.
The provider must perform a careful examination to rule out compartment syndrome and
neurovascular injuries.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs (AP and lateral views) typically are adequate to diagnose proximal tibia
metaphyseal fractures.
Advanced imaging studies rarely are obtained unless concern for proximal extension into the
physis exists.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management via a long leg cast is the main treatment option for low-energy
injuries in children younger than 10 years.

Nonsurgical Management
A well-padded long leg cast typically is applied with the leg in near-full extension with a
good varus mold to attempt to prevent post-fracture valgus deformity. The cast is
maintained for approximately 4 to 6 weeks, with serial radiographs obtained during the
first few weeks to ensure no fracture displacement occurs. Displaced fractures may be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:51 AM
AAOS | Tibial and Fibular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
3/18

managed via closed reduction with the patient under conscious sedation or anesthesia
before cast application. Most nondisplaced fractures are stable, and weight bearing may
be permitted as tolerated.
Surgical Management
Surgical management generally is reserved for high-energy, displaced proximal tibia fractures
in older children or for physeal involvement if acceptable closed reduction cannot be attained
or maintained.2
Fixation options for proximal tibia metaphyseal fractures include the following:
Percutaneous pinning with crossed Kirschner wires for fixation in younger patients, whether
closed or open reduction is necessary to achieve alignment
Plate fixation for older children and adolescent patients

Surgical Management
Open reduction may be required for displaced fractures in which closed reduction
cannot be maintained in a long leg cast because of interposed soft tissue or patient body
habitus. In these rare circumstances, a standard anteromedial approach to the proximal
tibia typically is used to facilitate removal of soft tissue and fracture reduction. The pes
anserine insertion also can be repaired via this approach if necessary. A long leg cast is
then applied if adequate reduction is achieved and can be maintained.
Complications
Genu valgum (Cozen phenomenon) is the most widely recognized sequela of low-energy
proximal tibia metaphyseal fractures (Figure 1).
Typically, no management is necessary acutely because these deformities often remodel and
improve spontaneously.
Neurovascular damage, compartment syndrome, and malunion may occur after high-energy
injuries.

extremity obtained at the time of injury demonstrates the fracture. B, Radiograph of bilateral
lower extremities obtained 3 years later demonstrates progressive valgus deformity.
(Reproduced with permission from Ramo B, Ellis HB: Lower extremity injuries, in Herring JA, ed:
Tachdjian’s Pediatric Orthopaedics: From the Texas Scottish Rite Hospital for Children, ed 6.
Philadelphia, PA, Elsevier, 2022, pp 1274-1360.)

Complications
Cozen phenomenon describes a valgus deformity of the tibia that occurs after a patient
sustains a nondisplaced proximal tibia metaphyseal fracture.1 Multiple theories have
been proposed for the etiology of this deformity; however, none have been proven in
the literature. The most accepted theory is an overgrowth phenomenon in which the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:51 AM
AAOS | Tibial and Fibular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
5/18

proximal tibia fracture stimulates the physis to grow while an intact fibula acts as a
tether, producing valgus angulation. The natural history of post-fracture valgus
deformity usually is apparent by 6 months postinjury and may progress for as long as 18
to 24 months post injury.3 Most children with Cozen phenomenon will have
spontaneous correction between 18 and 36 months postinjury.4 Bracing does not
improve this deformity and, therefore, is not recommended. Surgical management via
guided growth is reserved for patients with more than 10° of residual tibial valgus
deformity at 18 months postinjury.
Rehabilitation
A period of limited–weight bearing is recommended for 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively.
Kirschner wires typically are removed at approximately 4 weeks postoperatively, at which time
visible callous is observed and the fracture is nontender to palpation.
Return to activity usually occurs 12 weeks postoperatively after range of motion and strength
have normalized.
Outcomes
Valgus deformity may occur in as many as 50% to 80% of patients.5,6
Long-term follow-up studies indicate that most patients have spontaneous correction of their
mechanical axis and do not require additional surgical treatment.
Tibial and Fibular Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Tibial shaft fractures are among the most common injuries in children.
The severity of these injuries ranges from low-energy toddler fractures to high-energy open
fractures that may be associated with a high rate of compartment syndrome.
Most pediatric diaphyseal tibia fractures can be managed successfully nonsurgically; however,
injury type and patient factors may favor surgical management.
Tibial shaft fractures in nonambulatory children should increase suspicion for child abuse.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:51 AM
AAOS | Tibial and Fibular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
6/18

Epidemiology
Tibial shaft fractures are among the most common pediatric fractures. The mean age is 8
years, and the fractures are more common in males.7
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Relevant anatomy should be understood, including fascial compartments (anterior, lateral,
superficial posterior, deep posterior), vasculature, cross-sectional shape of the tibia, and
growth plates (Figure 2).
Neurovascular structures may be at risk because of direct injury or compartment syndrome.
The popliteal artery descends posteriorly and divides into the anterior and posterior tibial
arteries. The anterior tibial artery pierces the interosseous membrane proximally, at which
location it may be tethered and vulnerable to injury in patients with a proximal fracture.
The proximal tibia has two ossification centers: the proximal tibia physis (primary) and the
tibial tubercle apophysis (secondary), which are continuous with one another. Injury to the
tubercle growth plate via fracture or surgical management may result in a recurvatum growth
deformity.
The proximal tibia physis contributes approximately 6 mm/year of longitudinal growth and
closes at approximately age 14 years in females and age 16 years in males.
The distal tibia physis contributes approximately 4 mm/year of longitudinal growth and
generally closes between age 14 and 15 years.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
7/18

Figure 2 Cross-sectional illustration shows the anatomy at the mid-tibial level. The triangular
shape of the tibial shaft is important to consider in the placement of external fixator pins.
(Reproduced with permission from Eberson CP: Pediatric tibial fractures, in Flynn JM, Sankar WN,
Wiesel SW, eds: Operative Techniques in Pediatric Orthopaedic Surgery, ed 2. Philadelphia, PA,
Wolters Kluwer, 2016, pp 254-261.).
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
In young children, tibial shaft fractures commonly result from a twisting injury, in which the
body is rotated above a fixed foot.
In adolescents, these injuries usually result from a direct blow or high-energy injury, such as a
motor vehicle collision.
Associated Injuries
Approximately 30% of patients with a pediatric tibia shaft fracture have a concomitant fibular
fracture.8
Concomitant injuries of the ankle and foot commonly are associated with tibial shaft fractures,
especially distal third fractures.

Associated Injuries
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:51 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
8/18

Diaphyseal tibia fractures with associated fibular fractures tend to drift into valgus
because of the action of the muscles on the anterior and lateral compartments and the
lack of a lateral strut. Conversely, fractures of the tibia with an intact fibula tend to drift
into varus alignment.
Injury Classification
No commonly used classification system is available for tibial shaft fractures in children.
Tibial shaft fractures commonly are described based on several factors: open versus closed,
location of the fracture within the bone, fracture pattern, and comminution.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Patient presentation varies depending on the severity and mechanism of injury.
High-energy injuries require a complete trauma evaluation that follows Advanced Trauma Life
Support protocol.
Most children present with pain and tenderness at the fracture site and refusal to bear weight.
A focused physical examination should evaluate fracture displacement, skin integrity,
compartment swelling, and neurovascular status distal to the fracture site.
Unwitnessed spiral fractures should increase suspicion for child abuse, especially if the patient
is not of walking age.
Imaging Studies
Orthogonal radiographs of the tibia usually are adequate to diagnose a pediatric tibia shaft
fracture.
Dedicated images of the knee and ankle should be reviewed carefully to evaluate for physeal
involvement or concomitant ankle injury.
Comparison radiographs of the uninjured leg rarely are required but may help determine
length in patients with a severely comminuted fracture.
CT is indicated only if a high suspicion for physeal or articular involvement exists and
radiographs are insufficient.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:51 AM
AAOS | Tibial and Fibular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
9/18

If nonaccidental trauma is being considered in the differential diagnosis, a skeletal survey is
indicated to determine if other fractures in various stages of healing are present.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Most tibial fractures in children can be managed via closed reduction and long leg cast.
Healing takes 3 to 4 weeks for toddler fractures and 6 to 12 weeks for displaced fracture
patterns in older children and adolescents.
Indications
Nondisplaced fractures
Displaced, closed fractures amenable to closed reduction
Contraindications
Open fractures
Compartment syndrome
Floating knee injuries
Fracture pattern, body habitus, or skin integrity not amenable to closed management
Techniques/Procedures
Closed reduction and cast immobilization should be performed under appropriate sedation
and with fluoroscopic assistance.
Typically, a short leg cast is applied first, with an appropriate mold to decrease the likelihood
of fracture displacement.
The cast is then extended to an above-the-knee cast with the knee flexed approximately 45° to
control rotation at the fracture site and aid in maintaining non–weight-bearing status.
In the acute setting, especially if concern for swelling exists, the cast can be univalved or
bivalved to minimize the risk of cast-induced compartment syndrome.
The cast can be wedged between 7 to 14 days after swelling has decreased; however, this
may increase the risk of fracture displacement.
Patients may be admitted for observation and neurovascular monitoring, especially those with
a high-energy injury or considerable soft-tissue swelling.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:51 AM
AAOS | Tibial and Fibular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
10/18

Weekly radiographs are obtained for the first 2 to 3 weeks to ensure maintenance of
alignment.
The cast usually is changed to a short leg cast at approximately 4 to 6 weeks, at which time
radiographic signs of healing are observed. Immobilization is continued until radiographic
union.

Techniques/Procedures
Appropriate reduction should be planned before cast application. Because complete
tibia shaft fractures with an intact fibula tend to fall into varus, a valgus mold should be
applied. Conversely, complete tibia shaft fractures with a fractured fibula tend to fall into
valgus and recurvatum; therefore, a varus mold with the ankle in plantar flexion may
help prevent this deformity. To prevent malrotation, the tibial tubercle and the second
ray in the axial plane should be aligned during cast application. Avoiding excessive
dorsiflexion of the ankle during cast immobilization of distal third shaft fractures may
prevent recurvatum deformity at the fracture site. Acceptable deformity for tibial shaft
fractures are listed in Table 1.

Wilkins’ Fractures in Children, ed 9. Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2020.
Outcomes
SEND FEEDBACK

11/18

Closed reduction and cast immobilization is a safe and effective method to manage pediatric
tibial shaft fractures in most patients.9
Length of cast immobilization varies; however, mean time is 10 weeks.10
Surgical Management
Although most pediatric tibial shaft fractures are successfully managed via closed means,
surgical treatment is becoming more popular, especially in the adolescent patient population.
Methods of fixation include the following:
Percutaneous pinning
External fixation
Plate and screw fixation
Flexible intramedullary nailing
Rigid nailing (in skeletally mature adolescents)
Indications
Failure to maintain satisfactory alignment via closed techniques
Open fractures with marked soft-tissue injury
Severe swelling with concern for compartment syndrome
Fractures in large or obese children in whom the fracture may be difficult to control with the
use of a cast.
Floating knee injuries
Unstable and segmental fracture patterns
Polytrauma
Techniques/Procedures
Fixation is determined by fracture location, comminution, and the soft-tissue envelope.
External fixation
Indications
Fractures with extensive soft-tissue injury or compartment syndrome
Polytrauma patients
Flexible intramedullary nails (Figure 3)
Indications
Length-stable fractures in skeletally immature patients
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
12/18

The idea patient weighs less than 100 lb; however, flexible nails of appropriate diameter
may be indicated in heavier skeletally immature patients.
Percutaneous pinning
Indications
Noncomminuted, unstable oblique fractures
Rigid intramedullary nailing
Indications
Fractures in patients at or near skeletal maturity as determined by near or complete
closure of the tibial tubercle
Plate and screw fixation
Indications
Fractures with physeal or articular extension
Length-unstable fractures
Fractures not amenable to nail fixation because the fracture site is too proximal or distal to
achieve stability
The techniques for open reduction and plate fixation and for external fixation are the same as
those described for adult injuries.
Care must be taken to identify and avoid the physis with these techniques.

Figure 3 Images of the leg of a 6-year-old boy who was struck by a vehicle and sustained a grade
III open tibial shaft fracture. A, Clinical photograph shows the soft-tissue injury. B, Lateral
radiograph obtained in the trauma bay demonstrates a transverse displaced tibial shaft fracture.
C, Lateral fluoroscopic image shows the starting point distal to the proximal tibial physis. AP (D)
and lateral (E) fluoroscopic images show the final position of the flexible nails. Clinical photograph
(F) and AP (G) and lateral (H) radiographs obtained 2 months postoperatively. AP (I) and lateral (J)
radiographs obtained 7 months postoperatively demonstrate a healed fracture in near-anatomic
alignment. Hardware was removed without incident at 9 months postoperatively. (Courtesy of
Dustin Greenhill, MD, Bethlehem, PA.)
Preoperative Planning
Full-length radiographs should be carefully reviewed before selecting a fixation method.
Flexible nails are best indicated for length-stable middle-third fracture patterns in patients
with open physes.
The uninjured contralateral limb may be examined to help the surgeon determine appropriate
rotational alignment.
Selection of the proper nail size should be based on a target of 60% to 80% canal fill at the
tibial isthmus.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:51 AM
AAOS | Tibial and Fibular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
14/18

Patient Positioning
The patient is place in the supine position on a radiolucent table with a small bump placed
under the ipsilateral hip to maintain neutral rotation of the limb.
A small bump may help elevate the leg above the contralateral side to assist with lateral
fluoroscopic imaging.
Surgical Approach
Nails of the proper size are selected and pre-contoured to create a C-shape at the apex,
yielding three-point fixation.
The nails must be of the same diameter and material to create balanced fixation; in most
older children and adolescents, 3.0- to 4.0-mm diameter nails are used.
Fluoroscopy is used to localize the medial and lateral nail entry points.
The appropriate starting point is at least 1 cm distal to the proximal tibia physis and 2 cm
posterior to the tibial tubercle physis.
The skin incision should extend 2 to 3 cm proximally to allow for oblique passage of the nail
and prevent skin injury.
A drill or awl that is 1 to 1.5 mm larger than the diameter of the nail is used to enter the
intramedullary canal along the proposed path of the nail.
Care must be taken to not violate the far cortex.
The nails are inserted into the intramedullary canal and advanced to the level of the fracture
site.
The fracture is manually reduced, and the nails are sequentially passed across the fracture site
before driving them further into the distal segment.
The nails are then cut as close to the bone as possible, leaving 1 to 2 cm outside the bone to
facilitate later removal, if required.
The wounds are closed and a posterior splint, short leg cast, or walking boot is used for
stability.
Postoperative Management
For stable fracture patterns (>50% cortical contact), weight bearing may be initiated in reliable
patients.
Length unstable or comminuted fractures require non–weight bearing until callous is visible on
radiographs.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:51 AM
AAOS | Tibial and Fibular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004070
15/18

In general, weight bearing is permitted 4 to 6 weeks postinjury.
Removal of hardware, whether related to symptoms or elective, should be delayed until
complete healing is observed (approximately 6 to 12 months postoperatively).
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Unstable fracture patterns (ie, comminution) may lead to shortening or angulation, and
alternative fixation options should be considered.
Complications
Nonunion/Delayed Union
Delayed union and nonunion are rare but may occur in older children.11
Malunion
If closed reduction is not maintained, isolated tibia fractures typically drift into varus, and
combined tibia and fibula fractures drift into valgus.
Dissimilar from other long-bone fractures, remodeling of an angulated tibia shaft fracture
often is incomplete, requiring maintenance of near-anatomic alignment.7
Other Complications
Compartment syndrome may occur with open or closed fractures; however, it is less common
in children than in adults.
Compartment syndrome is more likely to occur after flexible nailing in patients who are heavy,
present with a neurologic injury, or have a comminuted tibial fracture.12
Rehabilitation
Few children with a tibial shaft fracture require extensive rehabilitation beyond basic crutch
training.
Outcomes
Despite the increasing popularity of surgical fixation, no studies to date have demonstrated a
clear advantage to flexible nailing over cast immobilization in pediatric patients with a tibia

fracture;13 failed cast immobilization is most common in patients with obesity, adolescents,
and patients with an unstable fracture pattern.9
